claim_verdicts.evidence: git show stage-1:DonHang.Api/Controllers/ProductsController.cs — line 9 `[Route("api/v1/products")]`; line 13 `[HttpGet]` on `List()`; line 22 `[HttpGet("{id:int}")]` on `Get(int id)`. Confirmed live on the running stage-1 lab: GET /api/v1/products -> 200 + array; GET /api/v1/products/1 -> 200 + single object.

git show stage-1:DonHang.Api/Controllers/OrdersController.cs — line 11 `[Route("api/v1/orders")]`; line 18 `[HttpPost]` on `Create(CreateOrderRequest request)`; line 30 `[HttpGet("{id:int}")]` on `Get(int id)`. Create also carries `[Authorize]` (line 17), which the lesson defers to a later lesson. No list-GET exists on the bare collection, matching the lesson's disclaimer.

Started the lab (docker compose, stage-1 images) and ran the lesson's two commands. `curl -i http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products` -> `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` + `[{"id":1,...}, ...8 products]`. `curl -i http://localhost:8080/api/v1/products/1` -> `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` + `{"id":1,"name":"Bàn phím cơ","priceVnd":1250000}` — an object, not an array. Caddyfile sends `handle /api/v1/*` to `reverse_proxy api:8080`, and host port 8080 is published, so the command works from the project root as written.

claim_verdicts.evidence: The claim attributes the collection/item split to convention, not to the spec; the spec half is what RFC 9110 settles. §9.1: "the standardized request methods in HTTP are not resource-specific... Once defined, a standardized method ought to have the same semantics when applied to any resource, though each resource determines for itself whether those semantics are implemented or allowed." §3.1 adds that HTTP vests "the request semantics in the request method". So HTTP attaches no collection/item restriction, as claimed.

git show stage-1:DonHang.Api/Controllers/OrdersController.cs lines 40-44: `[Authorize]`, `[HttpPatch("{id:int}/cancel")]`, `public async Task<ActionResult<OrderDto>> Cancel(int id)`, `var order = await orderService.CancelOrderAsync(id);`. With the class-level `[Route("api/v1/orders")]` that is PATCH /api/v1/orders/{id}/cancel. The action takes no request body, so the lesson's "the server decides what cancelling means" is true of this code.

git show stage-1:DonHang.Api/Controllers/AuthController.cs — line 10 `[Route("api/v1/auth")]`, line 13 `[HttpPost("login")]` on `Login(LoginRequest request)`, the class's only action (file ends line 25). `git ls-tree -r --name-only stage-1 | grep -i controller` returns exactly three controllers: Auth, Orders, Products. So `POST /api/v1/auth/login` and "its one endpoint" are both exact, and no plural-noun collection/item pair exists under /api/v1/auth.

ASP.NET Core routing docs, route-constraint table: "| `int` | `{id:int}` | `123456789`, `-123456789` | Matches any integer |" — negatives included; the docs do not state the 32-bit bound. Execution settles that half: on the running lab /api/v1/products/-1 returned 404 after 60ms (reached the action and the DB) while /api/v1/products/2147483648 and /api/v1/products/1.5 returned 404 in 0ms, logged by RequestLoggingMiddleware without ever reaching the action — the route itself did not match.

RFC 9110 §3.1 defines a resource as "the target of an HTTP request", identified by its URI; /api/v1/orders and /api/v1/orders/{id} are two distinct request targets (two distinct URIs), hence two distinct resources under the spec's own definition. Claim added and verified in this same round-3 pass, in response to this round's minor issue (section 4, the collection/item distinction was load-bearing but unlisted).

issues.quote: next to `/api/v1/orders`, the path Đơn Hàng already uses to create an order and to read one back by id
issues.text: Misdescribes the code and contradicts the lesson's own core point. At stage-1, `/api/v1/orders` (POST Create) creates an order; reading one back by id is `[HttpGet("{id:int}")]`, i.e. `/api/v1/orders/{id}` — a different URL, which section 4 then insists is a different resource ("two different resources, not two spellings of one path"). As written, the situation tells a junior the bare collection path serves GET-by-id, which is exactly what quiz q2 marks false.
issues.fix: Name both paths: "...but something about it doesn't sit right next to the order paths Đơn Hàng already has: `/api/v1/orders`, which creates an order, and `/api/v1/orders/1`, which reads one back by id."

issues.quote: collection URL — a URL naming every resource of one kind (`/api/v1/orders`); GET on it lists them all.
issues.text: Stated as an unconditional property of collection URLs, using the one example whose collection answers no GET at all. RFC 9110 §9.1: "each resource determines for itself whether those semantics are implemented or allowed." The How-it-works disclaimer ("not a promise that Đơn Hàng answers every branch of it today") comes a section later and does not reach this bullet.
issues.fix: Add the condition in the bullet: "...; GET on it, where a server offers one, lists them all."

issues.quote: `/api/v1/orders` and `/api/v1/orders/{id}` are two different resources, not two spellings of one path
issues.text: Unlisted claim: this is the lesson's load-bearing statement (outline item 2, the key of quiz q2) and no claim in .meta.json covers it. It is defensible — RFC 9110 §3.1 makes a resource "the target of an HTTP request", identified by its URI, and these are two targets — but the ledger should carry it so the source is on record instead of resting on the reader's goodwill.
issues.fix: Add to .meta.json claims, section 4: "A collection URL and an item URL under it are different request targets, hence different resources (RFC 9110 §3.1); splitting them into collection and item is REST convention, not an HTTP rule." The lesson sentence itself needs no change.

issues.quote: with `:int` saying only a whole number matches
issues.text: True as a necessary condition but incomplete: the constraint also rejects whole numbers outside the 32-bit range. Verified on the running lab — `/api/v1/products/2147483648` never reaches the action (404 logged in 0ms) while `/api/v1/products/-1` does (404 after a DB lookup). Claim 7 asserts the 32-bit bound; the lesson sentence does not, so a reader may assume any string of digits matches.
issues.fix: Write: "with `:int` saying only a whole number — one small enough to be a 32-bit integer — matches".
